match.reason: The closest bank point, eco-limits-gdp, is broader than this point: it also covers unpaid work, the environment and leisure, and it is written at an economics depth with real GDP and inflation terms, so it does not fit this Year 10 geography point on average income and wellbeing.

draft.title: GDP per person
card: Gross domestic product (GDP) is the total value of goods and services a country produces in a year.
GDP per person is GDP divided by the number of people. It shows the average income in a country.
It is an average, so it does not show how fairly income is shared. A few very rich people can raise it while many others stay poor.
It also says nothing directly about health or education. Two countries with the same GDP per person can differ in both.
draft.remember: GDP per person is an average income. It hides sharing, health and education.

a.q: What does a country's GDP per person tell us?
opts: Its average income for each person
How equally income is shared among people
How long people in it usually live
How many children go to school in it
a.why: GDP per person divides total output by the population, which gives an average income. It cannot show how income is shared, because an average hides differences between people.
a.clue: Think of what you get when you divide a total by the number of people.

b.q: Country P and Country Q both have a GDP per person of $20,000. In P, a few families earn most of the income. In Q, income is shared widely. What can be said?
opts: Their GDP per person is equal, but sharing differs
P is better off, because its richest people earn more
Q must have longer life expectancy than P
Their people must have the same wellbeing
b.why: The measure is the same, but it does not show how income is shared, and the two countries differ in that. It cannot prove that wellbeing is the same, nor that Q has longer life expectancy.
b.clue: An average can be the same when the spread is very different.

a.best: Its average income for each person

b.best: Their GDP per person is equal, but sharing differs

problems.detail: Two distractors use "must" ("must have the same wellbeing", "must have longer life expectancy"), while the card says countries "can" differ. These absolutes signal wrong answers, so a student can rule them out without knowing the idea.

The right option only restates facts in the stem: equal GDP per person, with income shared differently. A student can pick it without understanding that an average hides how income is spread, so the question is too easy for Year 10.

check.summary: The card and question a are sound. In question b, the right answer just restates the stem, and the wrong options give themselves away with "must", so it barely tests the idea.

b.q: Over ten years, Country R's GDP per person rose sharply. Almost all the extra income went to a few mine owners, and most workers earned no more. How is this possible?
opts: It is an average, so a few large gains can lift it
It shows the income of a typical worker in a country
It measures health and schooling as well as income
It divides GDP by the number of workers, not people
b.why: GDP per person is an average, so big gains for a few people can raise it even when most incomes stay flat. It is tempting to think it shows a typical worker's income, but an average hides how income is spread, which is why it rose here while most workers gained nothing.
b.clue: What happens to an average when a few values grow a lot?
